Candidate.full_text:
CANDIDATE ROLE INFORMATION

You are an ambitious sales professional negotiating a role with a young company. You care about income, but money isn't all that matters in life. You want room to build a career, protect time with your family, and avoid getting stuck in a role where your work is visible but you are not developing professionally.

Your objective is to reach an agreement with the highest total score you can, while recognizing that the Recruiter has priorities of their own that may conflict with yours. Every complete offer must include three terms: salary, a personal budget for work expenses such as client travel, meals, and lodging, and a starting date. The budget is an annual allowance for approved work expenses, not take-home pay. It lets you serve clients without paying those costs yourself; unused money stays with the company.

You prefer a higher salary and budget and an earlier start. Annual salary may range from $20,000 to $80,000: $20,000 gives you −2 points, $40,000 gives you 0, and $80,000 gives you +2. The personal budget may range from $1,000 to $20,000: $1,000 gives you −2, $10,500 gives you 0, and $20,000 gives you +2. Starting dates may range from 1 May to 30 September: 1 May gives you +2, around 16 July gives you 0, and 30 September gives you −2. The platform calculates intermediate scores automatically. For example, a $7,000 budget is worth about −0.74 points to you. You do not need to calculate this yourself.

These headline contract terms are easy to put numbers on. The interview also left you thinking about what the job would actually be like and what other terms you might ask for given what matters to you.

Background Information

On the way home, you think about the company's usual 30 vacation days per year and 3 remote-working days per week. Those arrangements seem reasonable. Each is worth 0 points to you. Still, more flexibility would mean more time with your family and more room for interests and professional development outside work, while less flexibility would work against those interests. For vacation, 10 days per year are worth −1 point to you and 50 days are worth +1. For remote work, 1 day per week is worth −1 and all 5 working days are worth +1. The two terms are scored separately, with proportional points for values in between.

You also remember the Recruiter's stories about how people grow in the company. One new hire attended an external professional training program; another was paired with an experienced mentor. Someone else built relationships with senior colleagues after volunteering at a recruitment fair. Those examples appealed to you because they offered concrete ways to learn and build relationships rather than vague promises of “growth.”

Other stories were less appealing. The Recruiter joked that sociable employees often end up organizing team events. Good client stories are turned into LinkedIn posts, and confident employees sometimes present at conferences. You enjoy people, but you do not want every spare hour turned into company visibility. A recruitment fair might expand your network; recurring publicity work might simply expand your workload.

That evening, your spouse asked whether the company would support the professional association that has helped you and what would happen if you eventually wanted to leave. Sponsored membership could help keep your skills and outside relationships alive. The question about leaving brought you back to the non-compete clause you had raised. You want to show commitment without unnecessarily limiting your future.

The interview contained small details and examples rather than a neat menu of contract features. Some may simply be background. Others could become useful terms if you connect them to what matters to you.

Your Task

Negotiate with the Recruiter by making offers in plain, ordinary language, as if you were writing them a short message. Every complete offer must include salary, a personal work-expense budget, and a starting date. You decide what else is worth discussing and when to raise it.

For example: “I propose a salary of [amount], a personal work-expense budget of [amount], and a starting date of [date], together with any other terms I choose to raise.” Use your own values and wording.

Your score is private and translates directly into the bonus payment you can earn from this task. You may propose an offer worth zero or less to you, but you can accept only an offer worth more than zero to you. An agreement requires both parties to accept the same offer, with a positive total score for each. Individual terms may still be worth zero or less. Without a deal, you will continue your job search; you do not have another offer in hand. This fallback is worth 0 points.

The researchers set the scoring rules in advance, and the platform applies them automatically; you do not assign points yourself. Each additional supported feature is worth between −1 and +1 points to you, based on the interests in your role. Its value to the Recruiter may differ. Separate commitments are scored separately, even when offered as one package; rewording the same term does not earn extra points. You are not limited to job features described or suggested here. You may creatively introduce other plausible job features or arrangements. If an idea has no scoring rule, the platform records it without adding points.

Recruiter.full_text:
RECRUITER ROLE INFORMATION

You are an ambitious Recruiter at a young company negotiating with a promising sales candidate. You care about making a strong hire, but filling the role isn't all that matters. You want to control costs, get the new hire productive quickly, keep the team working well, and avoid commitments that leave the company exposed if the hire does not work out.

Your objective is to reach an agreement with the highest total score you can, while recognizing that the Candidate has priorities of their own that may conflict with yours. Every complete offer must include three terms: salary, a personal budget for work expenses such as client travel, meals, and lodging, and a starting date. The budget is an annual allowance for approved work expenses, not take-home pay. It gives the new hire resources to serve clients; unused money stays with the company.

You prefer a lower salary and budget and an earlier start. Annual salary may range from $20,000 to $80,000: $20,000 gives you +2 points, $40,000 gives you 0, and $80,000 gives you −2. The personal budget may range from $1,000 to $20,000: $1,000 gives you +2, $10,500 gives you 0, and $20,000 gives you −2. Starting dates may range from 1 May to 30 September: 1 May gives you +2, around 16 July gives you 0, and 30 September gives you −2. The platform calculates intermediate scores automatically. For example, a $7,000 budget is worth about +0.74 points to you. You do not need to calculate this yourself.

These headline contract terms are easy to put numbers on. The interview also left you thinking about what hiring this person would actually involve, what the Candidate might ask for, and what other terms could benefit the company.

Background Information

Looking over your notes, you think about the company's usual 3-month probation period and 3-year contract. Those arrangements seem sensible. Each is worth 0 points to you. Still, the sales manager's description of the Candidate as “bright but raw” makes you cautious about committing too much before seeing how they perform. A longer probation gives the company more protection. For probation, no probation is worth −1 point to you and 6 months are worth +1. Contract length works in the other direction: 2 years are worth +1 point to you and 4 years are worth −1. The two terms are scored separately, with proportional points for values in between.

You also remember the Candidate's interest when you described the external professional training program and experienced employees who sometimes mentor new hires. Good development can turn a risky appointment into a strong performer and reflect well on your ability to spot talent. The Candidate was also curious about professional associations and recruitment fairs. Association sponsorship would cost the company money; a recruitment-fair role could help attract future candidates.

Other parts of the conversation suggested different possibilities. The Candidate was personable and might be good at organizing occasional team events. Their sales work could provide material for LinkedIn posts and other public communications. Conference presentations sounded less useful. Your manager sees them as costly distractions, and the Candidate did not seem eager to spend evenings preparing slides.

The Candidate's question about waiving the standard non-compete also stayed with you. You understand why future flexibility matters to them. But if they later leave for a competitor with knowledge of your clients, colleagues may ask why you gave up that protection. You want the new hire to develop and succeed without leaving the company unnecessarily exposed.
